bundled documentation. You must not search the internet, package registries, or any external
source for information about this project's source code. Even if you recognize what the
executable is, you must reimplement it from behavioral observation alone.

- Cloning or browsing the original GitHub repository, its forks, or mirrors
- Downloading the project from package registries: `cargo install <project>`, `go get github.com/<org>/<project>`, `pip install <project>`, `apt-get source <project>`, `npm install <project>`, etc.

Your submission must be a genuine reimplementation. The provided `./executable` is for
observation only — your final solution must not depend on it or any other pre-built version
of the same tool at runtime.

- Writing a wrapper script that delegates to the original binary (e.g., `exec zstd "$@"`)

through its normal user interface (CLI flags, stdin/stdout, etc.).

- You MUST NOT use strace, ltrace, or similar tracing/instrumentation tools on `./executable`

Note: this restriction applies ONLY to the provided `./executable`. You are free to use any
analysis tools on binaries that you produce yourself during development.

- Running the executable with any inputs, flags, and arguments to observe its behavior
- Reading any documentation files bundled in the workspace

# Clean and Immediate

Rhit works from your standard nginx logs, with no preparation.

You run it in your console, it leaves nothing behind, no temp file, no database.

# Instantly read your access log

You get an immediate overview with `rhit` or `sudo rhit` depending on your configuration

and from there you'll refine your query to get a more precise insight:

![intro](img/intro.png)

# Have new questions, and have them answered

With Rhit, you'll notice unexpected things in your logs. And you'll easily know more.

Here's an example:
Let's suppose you notice a [`413` HTTP code](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Status/413) in the status table.

You just have to type `rhit -s 413` to know why:

![413](img/status-413.png)

(I limit the tables displayed with `-f ref,path` in this screenshot in order to keep the image small)

# See the trends

You get an histogram per day of all the matching hits.

For each line in a table, you also get an histogram, in line, and a trend indicator.

And you can get tables of the most notable increases or decreases, for example here on referers:

![referer changes](img/referer-changes.png)

Of course you can filter, so you may focus for example on the new client errors, or on changes on your blog consultations.
</output>

# Log files

`rhit` (or `sudo rhit` depending on your configuration) will open the access logs if they're at their standard location.

So you just launch it as

```bash
rhit
```

and go on adding filters and fields as you explore your data.

You may open a specific file, or a specific directory, by giving the path as argument:

```bash
rhit my/archived/logs
```

**Note:**
    Only the default log format is currently supported. Custom logs aren't understood by Rhit.


# Launch parameters

`rhit --help` will display all available launch arguments.

The arguments you'll most often use enable

* [filtering](../usage-filters) hits to focus on a specific subset: `--date`, `--ip`, `--method`, `--path`, `--referer`, `--status`
* [choosing the displayed fields](../usage-fields): `--fields`
* [choosing the sorting key](../usage-key), either *hits* (default) or *bytes*: `--key`
* specifying the detail level, the length of tables: `--length`, from `0` (short) to `6` (long), `1` being the default
* seeing the [recent changes](../usage-changes): `--changes`
* [exporting](../export) the filtered lines, either to screen or to a file

# The fields argument

Here's a typical access log line:

```no-wrap
178.133.125.122 - - [21/Jan/2021:05:49:52 +0000] "HEAD /broot/download/x86_64-pc-windows-gnu/broot.exe HTTP/1.1" 200 0 "-" "Mozilla/4.0 (compatible; MSIE 6.0; Windows NT 5.1)"
```
Rhit can show tables on the following fields:

* date,
* time,
* method
* status
* (remote) IP
* referer
* path

You can specify the list of fields on which you want sorted tables.

If you specify nothing, the default is to show dates, status, referers and paths.

Fields are refered either by their name (eg `ip`) or by their initial (eg `i`).

The syntax is best explained with a few examples

Goal | Argument
-|-
Only the paths | `--field path` or `-f path` or `-f p`
IP and paths | `-f path+ip` or `-f p+i`
The default fields *and* the IP | `-f +ip` or `-f +i`
The default fields *and* IP and status | `-f +ip+status` or `-f +i+s`
The default fields minus dates | `-f -d`
The default fields with IP but not dates | `-f +i-d`
Default fields but paths moved to the end | `-f +p`
All fields except the paths | `-f all-paths` or `-f a-p`
All the fields, with dates moved to the end | `f all+dates` or `-f a+d`

# Date

This field is shown by an histogram.

You choose it with `--field date`, that you may shorten in `-f date` or `-f d`:

![date](img/fields-date.png)

By default the length of the bars is based on the hit counts (in pink). You may base it on sent bytes by changing the [sorting key](../usage-key).

# Time

This field is shown by an histogram with 24 bars: one per hour.

You choose it with `--field time`, that you may shorten in `-f d`.

Note that the time is the the server's time.

# Remote IP

The remote adresses table isn't displayed by default.

To see it alone use `rhit -f i`.
To see it with default fields, use `rhit -f +i`

![ip](img/fields-ip.png)

As for most fields, you see the number of different values (here the 24,691 remote adresses), the most frequent ones, of for each of them the hits, bytes sent, histogram per day and maybe a trend.

If you want more frequent adresses, use the `--length` field, for example `rhit -l 3`.

# Method

The HTTP method table isn't displayed by default.

To see it use `rhit -f +m`:

![method](img/fields-method.png)

As you'd see by [exporting the lines](../export) with `rhit -m other --lines`, the "other" methods are usually client errors, that is malformed requests.

# Path

The path is displayed by default.

If you want to see only the path, use `rhit -f p`:

![path](img/fields-path.png)

By default some paths are filtered from that tables: the images, scripts, etc.

If you don't want this filter, use the `--all` argument:

![path](img/fields-all-paths.png)

# Referer

The referer is one of the default fields. If you want ot see it alone, do `rhit -f ref`

*(yes, it's called "referer" and not "referrer" in the HTTP protocol, so I'll use this spelling everywhere in this documentation for consistency)*

![referer](img/fields-referer.png)

# Status

The status is one of the default fields. If you want ot see it alone, do `rhit -f status`

![status](img/fields-status.png)
</output>

# The filters arguments

While you may discover some big phenomenas when looking at the unfiltered tables, that's only the surface and you'll normally dive soon enough with filters either because the unfiltered data hinted a something interesting or because you wanted to look at some parts of your sites, or some errors, etc.

So there's a filter argument for each field, and they may be combined.

**Note:**
	On most shells, characters like `$`, `<`, `>`, `|`, or `!` have a special meaning if not between single quotes. In case of doubt put your arguments between quotes, for example `rhit -s '!404'`

# Filter by Date-Time

The date-time filter argument is `--date`, shortened in `-d`.

The order of tokens is year, month (numerical) then day (in 1-31).
If you specify the time, it follows the same logic: hour, minute, seconds.

For example here are the 6 days in the range from `2021/02/15` to `2021/02/20`:

![filter by date](img/filter-date.png)

The filter's behavior is probably better explained with a list of examples:

Purpose|Example
-|-
Show the hits of a specific day | `-d 2021/02/16`
Show the hits of a specific month | `-d 2021/02`
Show the hits of a specific year | `-d 2021`
All days but one | `-d '!2021/02/15'` (don't forget the quotes)
Days after a specific one | `-d '>2021/02/28'`
Days before a specific one | `-d '<2021/02/28'`
Days of a specific range (inclusive) | `-d 2021/11/01-2021/12/25`
Precise range (4 minutes)| `-d 2021/11/01T15:05-2021/11/01T15:08`
Very precise range (a few seconds)| `-d 2021/11/01T15:05:58-2021/11/01T15:06:04`

Shorcuts are sometimes possible. For example if all the log files are from the same year, you may ommit it:

![filter by date no year](img/filter-date-no-year.png)

# Filter by Time

To filter by the time in the day (in the server timezone), use `--time` or `-t`.

For example to get evening hits, use `-t '>18:30'`.

# Filter by Remote IP Address

Remote IP filters are defined with `--ip`, shortened in `-i`.

You may filter to show the hits of a specific IP or the other ones, or do a string based filtering.

Purpose|Example
-|-
Show the hits of a specific IP | `-i 35.180.167.230`
Show all hits but the ones of a specific IP | `-i '!35.180.167.230'`
Show all hits from IP starting with '192' | `-i '^192'`

# Filter by Method

Method filters are defined with `--method`, shortened in `-m`.

You may either filter to show the hits of a specific method or the other ones.

Purpose|Example
-|-
Show the hits of a specific method | `-m CONNECT`
Show all hits but the ones of a specific method | `-m '!POST'`

# Filter by Path

The path filter, defined with `--path` (or `-p`) is the most common one and the most powerful, with a versatile syntax.

The simplest path filter is just a word that the path must contain, for example `-p blog` when you want to see all hits on paths with "blog".

Example:

![filter og/h](img/filter-path-ogh.png)

But it may also be a regular expression, for example all paths with "download" and ending in "exe": `-p 'download.*exe$'`.

You may negate an expression with a `!`. For example all hits not ending in ̀"broot/": `-p '!broot/$'

You may add conditions by separating them with commas. To say you want all downloads, but not the exe and not rhit, you can say `-p download,!rhit,!exe$'

If your query is more complex, use parenthesis and logical operators `&`, `|` and `!` (add parenthesis around operators and parenthesis to avoid them being understood as part of regular expressions).

Here's a list of examples

Example | Meaning
-|-
`-p blog` | path contains "blog"
`-p 'blog.*broot'` | path contains "blog" and "broot", in this order
`-p 'blog,broot'` | path contains "blog" and "broot", in whatever order
`-p '^down/.*broot(.exe)?$'` | path starts with "down" and ends in "broot" with optionally "exe"
`-p 'down/(rh|bro)'` | path contains "down/" immediately followed by either "rh" or "bro"
`-p 'down/bro,!exe$'` | path contains "down/bro" and doesn't end in "exe"
`-p 'og | ( broot & !exe )'` | contains "og" or "broot" without "exe"
`-p '!^/\d+$'` | paths that aren't just a number
`-p '!^/\d+$,!broot'` | paths that aren't a number and don't contain "broot"
`-p 'y & !( \d{4} | sp | bl )'` | path contains "y" but neither a 4 digits number, "sp", nor "bl"

# Filter by Referer

Referer filters are specified with `--referer` or `-r`.

They follow exactly the same syntax than [path filters](#filter-by-path).

Example:

![filter by referer](img/filter-referer.png)

# Filter by Status

Status filters are specified with `--status` or `-s`.

The syntax is quite versatile.

Example | Meaning
-|-
`-s 404` | status is 404
`-s '!404'` | status is not 404
`-s 4xx` | status is of class 4xx (client error)
`-s '4xx,!404'` | status is of class 4xx (client error) but not 404
`-s 402-420` | status is between 402 and 420
`-s 3xx,401-405` | status is either in the 3xx class or from 401 to 405

# Combinations

Most often a unique filter isn't enough to study some event or phenomena.

You may want to answer a specific question, like what are the PHP files which aren't just some attacks:

```
rhit -p '\.php$' -s '!4xx'
```

Here are the possible values: * `tables`: the default summary, as tables * `raw`: raw lines as they appear in the source log files * `csv`: CSV * `json`: JSON All [filters](../usage-filters) apply, but the choice of fields isn't applied. For this documentation's screenshots, all outputs are filtered to keep 4 hits, by combining a date filter and a path filter: `-p 'poisson-frit' -d '2023/08/21'`. ## Tables Here's for example just the `paths` tables, with `-a` so that images aren't excluded: ![export tables](img/export-tables.png) ## Raw Use `rhit --output raw` or `rhit -o r` Without filter, this wouldn't be useful: this just unzips, sorts, and concatenates all log files. import datetime

for N in [3,4,5,6,7,8,9,10,15,20,25,30,35,40,60,80,100,150,200]:

            lines.append(f'1.2.3.4 - - [{day.strftime("%d/%b/%Y")}:05:49:52 +0000] "GET /p0 HTTP/1.1" 200 100 "ref0" "ua"')

import datetime
d0=datetime.date(2021,1,1)

def mk(name, rows):
    N=max(len(v) for _,v in rows)
    out=[]
    for d in range(N):
        for path,vals in rows:
            if d < len(vals):
                for i in range(vals[d]):
                    out.append(f'1.2.3.4 - - [{ds(d)}:05:49:52 +0000] "GET {path} HTTP/1.1" 200 100 "ref0" "ua"')
    open(name,"w").write("\n".join(out)+"\n")
N=30
mk("/tmp/e8/h30.log", [("/a",list(range(1,31))),("/b",[1]*30)])
mk("/tmp/e8/i30.log", [("/a",list(range(30,0,-1))),("/b",[1]*30)])
mk("/tmp/e8/j30.log", [("/a",[1]*30),("/b",list(range(30,0,-1)))])
mk("/tmp/e8/k30.log", [("/a",list(range(1,31))),("/b",list(range(31,61)))])
mk("/tmp/e8/l30.log", [("/a",list(range(1,31))),("/b",list(range(15,45)))])
mk("/tmp/e8/m30.log", [("/a",list(range(1,31))),("/b",list(range(1,31))[::-1])])
PY
for f in h30 i30 j30 k30 l30 m30; do printf "%-4s " $f; /workspace/executable --color no --silent-load -f p /tmp/e8/$f.log 2>&1 | sed -e 's/\x1b\[[0-9;]*m//g' | sed -n '7,8p' | python3 -c "
import sys
for l in sys.stdin.read().split('\n'):
    p=l.split('│')
    if len(p)>6 and p[1].strip(): print(p[2].strip(),p[3].strip(),p[5],repr(p[6]),end=' ;; ')
"; echo; done

{"command": "cd /tmp && cat > /tmp/e9/fit.py <<'PY'
import math
# /a: constant 1 hit/day ; /b: N..1  => /a percentage p[d] = 1/(N-d+1)
# observed arrow counts for /a:
obs={}
for N in range(8,42):
    if N<=9: c=0

    elif N<=22: c=2
    elif N<=37: c=1
    else: c=0
    obs[N]=c
def stats(y):
    n=len(y)
    avg=sum(y)/n
    last=y[-1]; first=y[0]
    half=n//2
    a1=sum(y[:half])/half if half else 0
    a2=sum(y[-half:])/half if half else 0
    # regression slope
    xb=(n-1)/2; yb=avg
    num=sum((x-xb)*(v-yb) for x,v in enumerate(y)); den=sum((x-xb)**2 for x in range(n))
    sl=num/den if den else 0
    # slope of last 3
    sl3=None
    if n>=3:
        yy=y[-3:]; xb=1; yb=sum(yy)/3
        num=sum((x-1)*(v-yb) for x,v in enumerate(yy)); den=2
        sl3=num/den
    return dict(n=n,chg=last-first,rel=(last-first)/first if first else 0,
                a1a2=a2-a1, sl=sl, sl3=sl3, last=last, first=first, avg=avg,
                ratio=last/first if first else 0, ratio_avg=last/avg if avg else 0)
print("N obs  chg    rel    a1a2   sl     ratio  ratio_avg")
for N in range(8,42):
    y=[1/(N-d+1) for d in range(N)]

{"command": "cd /workspace && cat > AGENT_REPORT.md <<'EOF'
# Rhit reimplementation - status report

## What is done (compiles, `./compile.sh` -> `./executable`)
* `src/inflate.rs` - self written DEFLATE/RFC1951 decoder + gzip (RFC1952) wrapper,
  no external crates (`cargo build --offline` works, zero dependencies).
* `src/main.rs` - CLI arg parsing skeleton, `--version` (`rhit 2.0.4`), `--help` header,
  gzip decompression, nginx log line parser (`parse_log_line`), the run-length
  "global date series" data model that rhit uses, and a small self-written regex engine
  used by the `--path` / `--referer` filters (supports `^ $ . \d \w \s [..] * + ? () |`).

## Reverse-engineered behaviour notes (verified against `./executable`)
* File discovery: recursive walk; a file is a "log file" when its **name contains
  `access.log`** (any suffix, incl. `.gz`) or when `--no-name-check` is given;
  the file is opened as gzip iff it ends with `.gz`; the **first line must parse**
  as a log line otherwise the file is skipped; if nothing is found -> `Error: NoLogFileFound`.
* Default log dir when no path argument: `/var/log/nginx`; if empty/missing it prints
  `No nginx log found at default location, do you have nginx set up?` + 2 more lines, exit 1.
* Errors are printed to stderr as `Error: <Debug of anyhow/enum>` with exit code 1:
  `PathNotFound("..")`, `NoLogFileFound`, `Io(Custom { kind: InvalidInput, error: "invalid gzip header" })`,
  `Io(Error { kind: InvalidData, message: "stream did not contain valid UTF-8" })`,
  `DateTime(IntExpected(ParseIntError { kind: Empty }))`, `DateTime(InvalidMonth(13))`,
  `TimeFilter(InvalidFormat)`, `TimeFilter(TimeParse(IntExpected(ParseIntError { kind: InvalidDigit })))`,
  `StatusFilter(ParseInt(ParseIntError { kind: InvalidDigit }))`,
  `StrFilter(InvalidPattern("& blog", "unexpected '&'"))` and
  `StrFilter(InvalidRegex(Syntax(\n~~~\nregex parse error:\n    <pat>\n    ^\nerror: <msg>\n~~~\n)))`.
* Terminal width: real tty width, **50 when stdout is not a tty**.
* Summary line: `<hits> hits and <bytes> from <min date> to <max date>` where
  hits is fg 204, the dates fg 11 + bold; dates are the first/last entry of the
  *global run-length* date series (dates are appended in file order, a new entry is
  created whenever the date differs from the previous line's date - this is why
  repeated date blocks appear in the date table).
* Byte formatting: < 10000 printed as-is, otherwise `<n>K` (K = 1000, rounded to 2 digits).
* Filter messages are printed after the summary, one paragraph per filter, in the
  order date, remote address, time, method, path, referer, status:
  `Filtering by <field> on pattern <pat> removed <pct>% of total lines` then
  ` ==> hits: <n>, bytes sent: <n>`. Percentages are relative to the *unfiltered* total.
  Paragraphs are wrapped at the terminal width with the algorithm described in main.rs.
* Table detail levels (`-l 0..6`) limits: ip 3/5/20/30/40/50/60,
  referer 5/10/40/60/80/100/120, path 10/50/100/150/200/250/300.
  `-l 0` replaces the status table by a `2xx/3xx/4xx/5xx` percentage summary table.
* Row sparkline: chars ` ▁▂▃▄▅▆▇`, `idx = round(v/max*7)`, 0 -> space;
  it covers the **global** date entries, and is truncated to the **last 20 entries**
  when there are more; the cell is right aligned when the column is wider than the
  sparkline and wraps (right aligned) when narrower.
* Sparkline column width = min(20, nb entries), squeezed so the whole table fits the
  terminal width exactly.
* When the sparkline ("days") column is present, the ip/ref/path tables drop the `%` column.
* Field table headings: `<n> methods. `, `<n> HTTP status codes. `, `<n> remote IP addresses. `,
  `<n> referrers. `, `<n> paths (excluding resources like images, css, etc.). `
  followed by `<limit> most frequent:` when truncated (with `-a` the exclusion note disappears).
* `-o raw` re-prints the original lines sorted by (date,time); `-o csv` writes
  `date,time,remote address,method,path,status,bytes sent,referer` with path/referer always quoted;
  `-o json` pretty prints objects with keys date,time,remote_addr,method,path,status(string),bytes_sent(number),referer.
* Progress bar (unless `--silent-load`): repeated `\x1b[7\x1b[2K<n> / <total> \x1b[48;5;5m\x1b[38;5;11m` +
  40 cells (filled = floor(progress*40) `█`, rest spaces) + `\x1b[49m\x1b[39m\x1b[8`, followed by
  `I've read 1 file in "x.log"` / `I've read N files in ["a", "b"]`.

## TODO / not implemented yet
1. **Table rendering + summary + filter messages are not wired to `main` yet** - the
   pieces are there (parsers, data model, regex) but `run()` currently stops after
   printing the version. Needs: apply filters, print summary/filter messages, render
   the 7 field tables with the exact column widths/colours/alignment observed, render
   `--changes` tables, implement `-k bytes` histogram scaling, `-l` limits, `-a`.
2. Help table body (`HELP_ROWS` is empty) - the exact rows/colours are in /tmp/help.txt.
3. Time-filter grammar: only `>HH[:MM[:SS]]`, `<HH...>`, `HH-HH` (2-digit hours,
   minutes/seconds must be 2 digits); bare times are `Error: TimeFilter(InvalidFormat)`.
4. Date-filter grammar: `YYYY[/MM[/DD]][T HH:MM:SS]`, 1..3 components, `!`, `>`, `<`,
   `A-B` inclusive; the `T` part must be complete (`HH:MM:SS`) and matches exactly.
5. Status filter: `N`, `Nxx`, `!`, `A-B`, comma separated list; `1xx` is a parse error.
6. Method filter: exact match (case sensitive), `none` = lines whose request field is
   empty, `other` = a method outside {GET,HEAD,POST,PUT,DELETE,CONNECT,OPTIONS,TRACE,PATCH}.
7. IP filter: plain **prefix** match on the IP string, optional leading `^`, `!` negates,
   no comma list.
8. **The per-row "trend" column logic is not reverse engineered yet.** Observed facts:
   arrows `➚` / `➘`, 0..3 arrows centred in the cell, direction follows the row's
   share of the daily total, magnitude thresholds roughly at ratios 2.4 / 5.2 / 32
   (up) and 0.47 / 0.20 / 0.027 (down), but several shapes deviate (see /tmp/e9 notes).
   Needs more experiments.
9. Known methods set assumption {GET,HEAD,POST,PUT,DELETE,CONNECT,OPTIONS,TRACE,PATCH}
   needs verification (it produced the expected 9+`other` buckets in tests).
EOF

cd /workspace && cat > AGENT_REPORT.md <<'EOF'
# Rhit reimplementation - status report

## What is done (compiles, `./compile.sh` -> `./executable`)
* `src/inflate.rs` - self written DEFLATE/RFC1951 decoder + gzip (RFC1952) wrapper,
  no external crates (`cargo build --offline` works, zero dependencies).
* `src/main.rs` - CLI arg parsing skeleton, `--version` (`rhit 2.0.4`), `--help` header,
  gzip decompression, nginx log line parser (`parse_log_line`), the run-length
  "global date series" data model that rhit uses, and a small self-written regex engine
  used by the `--path` / `--referer` filters (supports `^ $ . \d \w \s [..] * + ? () |`).

## Reverse-engineered behaviour notes (verified against `./executable`)
* File discovery: recursive walk; a file is a "log file" when its **name contains
  `access.log`** (any suffix, incl. `.gz`) or when `--no-name-check` is given;
  the file is opened as gzip iff it ends with `.gz`; the **first line must parse**
  as a log line otherwise the file is skipped; if nothing is found -> `Error: NoLogFileFound`.
* Default log dir when no path argument: `/var/log/nginx`; if empty/missing it prints
  `No nginx log found at default location, do you have nginx set up?` + 2 more lines, exit 1.
* Errors are printed to stderr as `Error: <Debug of anyhow/enum>` with exit code 1:
  `PathNotFound("..")`, `NoLogFileFound`, `Io(Custom { kind: InvalidInput, error: "invalid gzip header" })`,
  `Io(Error { kind: InvalidData, message: "stream did not contain valid UTF-8" })`,
  `DateTime(IntExpected(ParseIntError { kind: Empty }))`, `DateTime(InvalidMonth(13))`,
  `TimeFilter(InvalidFormat)`, `TimeFilter(TimeParse(IntExpected(ParseIntError { kind: InvalidDigit })))`,
  `StatusFilter(ParseInt(ParseIntError { kind: InvalidDigit }))`,
  `StrFilter(InvalidPattern("& blog", "unexpected '&'"))` and
  `StrFilter(InvalidRegex(Syntax(\n~~~\nregex parse error:\n    <pat>\n    ^\nerror: <msg>\n~~~\n)))`.
* Terminal width: real tty width, **50 when stdout is not a tty**.
* Summary line: `<hits> hits and <bytes> from <min date> to <max date>` where
  hits is fg 204, the dates fg 11 + bold; dates are the first/last entry of the
  *global run-length* date series (dates are appended in file order, a new entry is
  created whenever the date differs from the previous line's date - this is why
  repeated date blocks appear in the date table).
* Byte formatting: < 10000 printed as-is, otherwise `<n>K` (K = 1000, rounded to 2 digits).
* Filter messages are printed after the summary, one paragraph per filter, in the
  order date, remote address, time, method, path, referer, status:
  `Filtering by <field> on pattern <pat> removed <pct>% of total lines` then
  ` ==> hits: <n>, bytes sent: <n>`. Percentages are relative to the *unfiltered* total.
  Paragraphs are wrapped at the terminal width with the algorithm described in main.rs.
* Table detail levels (`-l 0..6`) limits: ip 3/5/20/30/40/50/60,
  referer 5/10/40/60/80/100/120, path 10/50/100/150/200/250/300.
  `-l 0` replaces the status table by a `2xx/3xx/4xx/5xx` percentage summary table.
* Row sparkline: chars ` ▁▂▃▄▅▆▇`, `idx = round(v/max*7)`, 0 -> space;
  it covers the **global** date entries, and is truncated to the **last 20 entries**
  when there are more; the cell is right aligned when the column is wider than the
  sparkline and wraps (right aligned) when narrower.
* Sparkline column width = min(20, nb entries), squeezed so the whole table fits the
  terminal width exactly.
* When the sparkline ("days") column is present, the ip/ref/path tables drop the `%` column.
* Field table headings: `<n> methods. `, `<n> HTTP status codes. `, `<n> remote IP addresses. `,
  `<n> referrers. `, `<n> paths (excluding resources like images, css, etc.). `
  followed by `<limit> most frequent:` when truncated (with `-a` the exclusion note disappears).
* `-o raw` re-prints the original lines sorted by (date,time); `-o csv` writes
  `date,time,remote address,method,path,status,bytes sent,referer` with path/referer always quoted;
  `-o json` pretty prints objects with keys date,time,remote_addr,method,path,status(string),bytes_sent(number),referer.
* Progress bar (unless `--silent-load`): repeated `\x1b[7\x1b[2K<n> / <total> \x1b[48;5;5m\x1b[38;5;11m` +
  40 cells (filled = floor(progress*40) `█`, rest spaces) + `\x1b[49m\x1b[39m\x1b[8`, followed by
  `I've read 1 file in "x.log"` / `I've read N files in ["a", "b"]`.

## TODO / not implemented yet
1. **Table rendering + summary + filter messages are not wired to `main` yet** - the
   pieces are there (parsers, data model, regex) but `run()` currently stops after
   printing the version. Needs: apply filters, print summary/filter messages, render
   the 7 field tables with the exact column widths/colours/alignment observed, render
   `--changes` tables, implement `-k bytes` histogram scaling, `-l` limits, `-a`.
2. Help table body (`HELP_ROWS` is empty) - the exact rows/colours are in /tmp/help.txt.
3. Time-filter grammar: only `>HH[:MM[:SS]]`, `<HH...>`, `HH-HH` (2-digit hours,
   minutes/seconds must be 2 digits); bare times are `Error: TimeFilter(InvalidFormat)`.
4. Date-filter grammar: `YYYY[/MM[/DD]][T HH:MM:SS]`, 1..3 components, `!`, `>`, `<`,
   `A-B` inclusive; the `T` part must be complete (`HH:MM:SS`) and matches exactly.
5. Status filter: `N`, `Nxx`, `!`, `A-B`, comma separated list; `1xx` is a parse error.
6. Method filter: exact match (case sensitive), `none` = lines whose request field is
   empty, `other` = a method outside {GET,HEAD,POST,PUT,DELETE,CONNECT,OPTIONS,TRACE,PATCH}.
7. IP filter: plain **prefix** match on the IP string, optional leading `^`, `!` negates,
   no comma list.
8. **The per-row "trend" column logic is not reverse engineered yet.** Observed facts:
   arrows `➚` / `➘`, 0..3 arrows centred in the cell, direction follows the row's
   share of the daily total, magnitude thresholds roughly at ratios 2.4 / 5.2 / 32
   (up) and 0.47 / 0.20 / 0.027 (down), but several shapes deviate (see /tmp/e9 notes).
   Needs more experiments.
9. Known methods set assumption {GET,HEAD,POST,PUT,DELETE,CONNECT,OPTIONS,TRACE,PATCH}
   needs verification (it produced the expected 9+`other` buckets in tests).
EOF
timeout 300 ./compile.sh 2>&1 | tail -3; ls -la executable 2>/dev/null | head -2; ./executable --version

## Summary

**What I did:** I reverse-engineered `./executable` (which turned out to be **rhit 2.0.4**, a nginx-log analyzer) purely by running it and reading the bundled `website/` documentation, then wrote an original Rust codebase.

**Key discoveries (all verified by experiment):**
- Log-file discovery: recursive walk, files whose *name contains* `access.log`, `.gz` read as gzip, the **first line must parse** else the file is silently skipped.
- Error messages/exit codes: `Error: PathNotFound("â¦")`, `NoLogFileFound`, gzip/UTF-8 `Io(...)` variants, `DateTime(...)`, `TimeFilter(...)`, `StatusFilter(...)`, `StrFilter(...)` (exact Debug formatting captured).
- The **global date series is a run-length Vec built in file order** (a new entry whenever the date differs from the previous line) â this explains the duplicated date rows and why the summary's from/to dates follow the last row's range.
- Terminal width = real tty width, **50 when piped**; the exact word-wrapping algorithm of headings/filter messages.
- Sparkline levels `" âââââââ"` with `idx = round(v/max*7)`; row histograms cover the global entries truncated to the **last 20**; column widths fill the terminal exactly; level limits for ip/ref/path at `-l 0..6`.
- Exact ANSI colour spans for the summary line, table borders/headers/cells, filter messages and the progress bar (`\x1b[7\x1b[2Kâ¦\x1b[8`).

**Code produced:** `src/inflate.rs` (self-written DEFLATE/RFC1951 + gzip wrapper) and `src/main.rs` (arg parsing, `--version`/`--help` header, log parser, run-length data model, small regex engine for path/referer filters) â **zero external crates**, builds with `cargo build --offline`, and `./compile.sh` produces a working `./executable`.

**Limitations:** the table rendering / filter-message / changes-table rendering is not yet wired into `run()` and the per-row **trend** column logic is not fully reverse-engineered (thresholds partially mapped). All of this, plus the exact remaining grammars, is documented with reproducible observations in `AGENT_REPORT.md` for hand-off. Build artifacts are git-ignored and committed state is clean.
